lessons.title: What red offal is and how to keep it with its carcass
lessons.html:
What red offal is

Offal is the parts of the animal that are not the carcass. Red offal is the dark red organs from the chest and belly. It is sold as food, so it must be handled as cleanly as meat.

Red offal includes

  • Heart
  • Liver
  • Lungs
  • Kidneys
  • Spleen
  • Tongue and head meat (in many abattoirs)

The heart, lungs and liver are often taken out together. This set is called the pluck.

Keep the offal with its carcass

The meat inspector must look at the red offal of every animal. The inspector checks for signs of disease, such as cysts, abscesses or worms. If there is a problem in the offal, the inspector may also need to look again at the carcass it came from.

So every set of offal must stay linked to its carcass:

  • Hang it on the hook or tray with the same number as the carcass.
  • Keep it in the right order on the offal rail or tray line.
  • Never move offal to another hook or tray until the inspector has passed it.

Example

Thandi takes the pluck from carcass 57 and hangs it on hook 57. The inspector finds a cyst in the heart. Because the hook number matches, the inspector can go straight to carcass 57 and check it.

If offal gets mixed up, the inspector cannot know which carcass is sick. Then many carcasses may have to be held or condemned. That is a big loss for the abattoir and the farmer.

lessons.title: Cleaning, cooling and hygiene for red offal
lessons.html:
Cleaning, cooling and hygiene

After inspection

  1. Wait until the meat inspector has passed the offal.
  2. Separate the organs: heart, lungs, liver, kidneys.
  3. Trim away bits marked by the inspector, fat and blood clots, as your abattoir instructions say.
  4. Rinse with clean, cold water if your procedure says so.
  5. Put the offal on clean trays or hang it on clean hooks.
  6. Take it to the chiller quickly. Offal spoils faster than meat.

Condemned offal

Offal that the inspector rejects is condemned. It goes into the marked condemned bin only. It must never be mixed with good offal or taken home. Condemned material can spread disease.

Hygiene rules

  • Wash your hands before you start, after breaks, and after touching anything dirty.
  • Wear a clean white overall, apron, hairnet and boots.
  • Sterilise your knife in the hot water sterilizer between animals.
  • Never let offal touch the floor. If it falls, tell your supervisor. It may have to be trimmed or condemned.
  • Keep good offal away from the gut (rough offal) area.
  • Do not eat, smoke or chew gum in the work area.

Safety

  • Cut away from your body.
  • Wear a steel mesh glove on the hand that does not hold the knife, if your abattoir provides one.
  • Keep your knife sharp. A blunt knife slips.
  • Report any cut, even a small one, so it can be cleaned and covered.

Key points

  • Red offal is heart, liver, lungs, kidneys and spleen.
  • Keep every set of offal on the hook or tray with its carcass number.
  • Only handle and separate offal after the inspector has passed it.
  • Condemned offal goes into the condemned bin only.
  • Chill offal quickly because it spoils fast.

quiz.question: Which of these is red offal?

options.text: The heart, lungs and liver taken out together

quiz.question: Why must offal stay on the hook with the same number as its carcass?

options.text: So the inspector can link any disease to the right carcass

quiz.question: What should you do if a piece of offal falls on the floor?

options.text: Pick it up and put it back
Rinse it and send it to the chiller

quiz.question: Offal spoils faster than meat, so it must be chilled quickly.
You may move offal to another hook before the inspector has passed it.
Which are good hygiene rules when handling red offal? (select all that apply)
